OpenAI has now paused training of its latest models for the second time in three months this time because its AI agents went rogue while searching federal government websites.  The incident follows a similar halt in July after a cyberattack on Hugging Face. What started as simple instruction-following quickly crossed into unsafe territory once agents gained access to real tools, APIs, and external systems.  This is more than a training setback. It’s a clear signal that the risks in AI are shifting from what models know to what they can actually do in the real world.  @trishoolai highlights why this matters for the next layer of defense:  • Input Guards block malicious prompts before they reach the model • Output Guards catch unsafe responses before they’re released • Future layers will focus on agent identity, credential protection, least-privilege access, and sandboxed tool calls  Trishool’s work on SN23 shows a promising path forward: securing not just what enters and leaves AI, but what it can do all powered by decentralized intelligence. A thoughtful step toward safer, more trustworthy AI for everyone.

Bitget has actively worked to restore liquidity by bringing its user protection reserves back up to roughly $309 million using internal company capital while rolling out phased withdrawals for customers. 🔎 Deep dive on cloud security  Binary Security’s Haakon Wik Gulbrandsrud reports five critical Azure API Connections flaws that enabled cross-tenant access to connected services, including Key Vault and Azure SQL.  His new write-up traces a series of vulnerabilities and patch bypasses. Azure’s shared API Management layer routes connector requests and substitutes the credentials stored for the selected connection.  → Path traversal redirected requests from an attacker’s connection to another tenant’s, enabling Key Vault secret reads. → An undocumented endpoint exposed a similar route to arbitrary SQL queries. → A later bypass worked because validation checked a URL before its path was normalized. The runtime and router disagreed about which connection the request targeted. → Fixing that bypass reopened an earlier runtime URL attack.  Gulbrandsrud reports $200,000 in total bounties and says all five vulnerabilities were fixed. Access depended on the permissions of the targeted connection’s backend credentials.  Microsoft’s advisory for one finding, CVE-2026-21227, confirms that it is fully mitigated and requires no customer action.  binsec.no/posts/2026/10/one-… msrc.microsoft.com/update-gu…

CVE-2026-104286 is a zero-day path traversal in FortiMail actively exploited in the wild with no patch available. Unauthenticated attackers are writing files outside intended directories to achieve remote code execution and full mail gateway compromise.  Key findings:  - CVE-2026-104286 affects FortiMail 7.2 through 8.0.1 across all current release lines. Exploitation is unauthenticated: a crafted request abuses the IBE feature to write arbitrary files outside the intended directory, which attackers are leveraging to drop malicious binaries and a modified ld[.]so.preload for persistent, system-wide code injection on every process launch. No patch exists. Fortinet's current guidance is to disable the IBE feature via CLI (config system encryption ibe / set status disable / end) or restrict management interface access to trusted private networks only.  - Post-exploitation forensic artifacts are well-defined. Look for the following added or modified files on disk: /data/lib/liblog.so (SHA256: 8015f34dc84922b03688399d7f9fe7a00361789f7e420c7e2a2cdb23e75cef84), /data/bin/webconsole (SHA256: 7a6cea9f5c9e2e9994d4e3c4da73f86cf5acd05ea5d312c066c9d1dafd69ee38), /data/bin/mailservice (SHA256: 4000276a150a165d3c2537d1e19fb393c4de8333076a16655e28059cae82157b), a modified /bin/smit (SHA256: 77324ac428bde86d351fc5fc06f6d64a6bfe737dfb2743df1d4c5ac2418a5b6a), and critically /data/etc/ld.so.preload (SHA256: 8953ec7960b09f544a880b072ad4e6cfda7a8303f486251d3478dcfdfbac23b6). A modified /data/migadmin.tar.gz and /data/etc/httpd.conf round out the tampered file set.  - The attacker established data exfiltration via a rogue archive account. Log evidence shows an "archive234" account added through CLI with rotation to a remote IP at 79.141.169[.]187 via the config system archive path, rotating stored mail to /uploads. A second IP, 45.129.0[.]192, appears in the IOC set. The cron-triggered shell command visible in logs (type=event subtype=system pri=debug user=system ui=cron msg="(root) CMD (/bin/sh -c 'O=/migadmin...") shows persistence operating through scheduled execution. Cisco published a critical SD-WAN Manager advisory on Wednesday. CISA added it to KEV the same day.  CVE-2026-76504. CVSS 9.8.  Cisco's summary: an "unauthenticated, remote attacker" could reach the system "with privileges of the admin user."  The cause is small. A URI-encoded request slips past an authentication rule meant to protect one API endpoint.  Cisco's IOC examples show one encoded letter: %6a in place of the letter j in j_security_check. Cisco also says any single encoded character works. Grep for %6a alone and you can miss it.  Three lines from the advisory decide the weekend:  "In September 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability."  "There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability."  "This vulnerability affects Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, regardless of system configuration."  No workaround. The only mitigation Cisco lists is to let only known, trusted hosts reach the manager, and Cisco calls that temporary. Active exploitation. The KEV deadline for US federal agencies is October 3.  First fixed releases: 20.9 -> 20.9.10.1 20.12 -> 20.12.8.2 20.15 -> 20.15.6.1 20.18 -> 20.18.4.1 26.1 -> 26.1.2.1 26.2 -> 26.2.1 Older than 20.9: migrate. Cisco-managed SD-WAN Cloud is already fixed, no action needed.  Before you patch, check the logs Cisco names: serviceproxy-access.log and vmanage-server.log, requests to j_security_check from addresses you do not recognize, and in vmanage-server.log users whose names start with viptela-reserved-. Cisco warns these entries can also appear in normal operation, so compare against your baseline.  Patching closes the door. It does not tell you whether someone already walked through it.  The manager holds the policy for every edge in the fabric. Admin on the manager is, in practice, admin on the WAN.  Cisco says it was found while resolving a TAC support case. If you run SD-WAN Manager, this is the weekend change window.

sample_tweets.text: BPFDoor, Rekoobe, and a new Linux implant called AVERAT are hitting telecom edge appliances and mail-security gateways across South Korea 🇰🇷 and Taiwan 🇹🇼, using SMTP port 25 as C2 camouflage and fileless staging to survive on embedded devices with no on-disk trace.  Key findings:  - The attack chain opens with a dropper (SHA-256: 2bedc26d4b29b435c21962beed7db21188a0219a0d28334bba8b4fb1656d7b15) that derives its AES-128-ECB key from SHA1("ShareTech"), pointing squarely at ShareTech appliances. It copies two binaries from /addpkg/sbin/ into /sbin as ntpdate and udevds, executes them, then unlinks both within ten seconds. Both processes keep running without an on-disk image: /proc/pid/exe resolves to "(deleted)" and grepping /sbin finds nothing. The dropper re-executes as a watchdog and relies on the firmware's own package startup to survive reboots, so there is no persistence code to find. Gate artifacts to hunt: /tmp/flag (precondition), /HDD/ms6x2xTo64/updIptable.php (shell script disguised as PHP), and /HDD/ms6x2xTo64/execProcEnd (watchdog marker).  - AVERAT (six builds, all recovered from /sbin/udevds) connects outbound on TCP/25, issues EHLO and STARTTLS, then runs its own hand-rolled TLS session authenticated with magic value 1571 (0x0623). Check-ins occur every 600-699 seconds and persist the interval to a hidden state file: /var/lib/.db, /var/lib/.sencha, /var/lib/.us, or /var/lib/.a depending on build. The 276-byte encrypted config blob (RC4, key derived from its own first 16 bytes) holds three C2 host/port slots. C2 infrastructure splits between attacker-registered domains (mx.zxopfds[.]com, spam.suwaccqi[.]com, mx1.wwstifsteel[.]com) and hardcoded consumer-broadband IPs (59.125.211[.]65, 122.116.138[.]33, 1.34.200[.]85) confirmed as compromised Chunghwa Telecom HiNet (AS3462) CPE: a fuel retailer's Synology NAS, an end-of-life NetKlass SMB appliance, and a Dahua DH-XVR5116HS-I3 CCTV recorder. All three also run operator-installed PPTP on 1723 with a byte-identical banner, making each node a dual-purpose relay and VPN foothold. Command code 1618 opens a proxy or port-forward through the compromised appliance; the reboot handler (code 916) calls sync() before forcing a kernel restart, deliberately flushing volatile state while leaving disk persistence intact.  - The South Korean 🇰🇷 BPFDoor cluster (SHA-256: a37ea9897221d4495b538de72b74f2aa1d2ff09b7b6dcedd395aee58931adbf3 and 7e667ba5f9df912e02275d3cfe3809d16f822fe776f4035c84b118ebd925b1b5) uses magic bytes 0x6693 (UDP), 0x4274 (TCP), and 0x7820 (ICMP), passwords gZbpx0 (reverse shell) and sT21xf (bind shell), and impersonates /var/run/spamsniper.pid, directly naming SpamSniper anti-spam software as the masquerade target. The data-plane BPFDoor pair (a6f3b7f932761fb1fd5e74123f2482e36c65dd13e769af2ce08c65da195bfa7a and 4435fcd6862921092614dbeaa880e4192352984686ebcd98f0ba13ee8e226ef9) spoofs ora_ppmond and /sniper/snipe/bin/dtnpd respectively, integrating Tiny Shell with single-byte S/U/D commands for shell, upload, and download. The BPF Rekoobe sample (652508a9cf40bee883dc0e5e219dfeba71fe7dac591d01c89f74c21f73b4963f) sniffs for traffic where src port and dst port both equal 25, authenticated with a 32-byte magic sequence and XOR key uvTIgh47,[@]R, then spoofs /sniper/autorun/rblsmtpd to blend with a mail gateway's expected process list. On a SpamSniper appliance, a packet with src=25 dst=25 matches the legitimate MTA relay firewall rule and reaches the raw socket before stateful inspection.  - The updated BPFDoor controller now supports HTTPS POST tunneling (-g flag, dogetlogin function) to defeat static network signatures: it sends mathematically padded requests (e.g., POST /admin/login.aspx?id=99990) so the string "9999" lands at exactly offset 26 of the TCP payload as a dynamic reference point. The controller spoofs /usr/sbin/abrtd via PR_SET_NAME. New flags include -H for a hidden relay IP, -D to customize URI paths for log blending, and -v for debug output. MITRE ATT&CK techniques documented across both clusters include T1205.002 (Socket Filters), T1036.004/T1036.005 (Masquerading), T1070.003 (Clear Command History), T1071.003 (Mail Protocols), T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography), T1090 (Proxy), and T1584.008 (Compromise Infrastructure: Network Devices), among others in the report.  Takeaway for responders: File-based detection on these appliances will fail because nothing survives in /sbin. Hunt for Linux processes where /proc/pid/exe shows "(deleted)", inspect memory maps for executable pages with no backing file, and alert on the process-tree sequence of sh -c against a .php path followed by cp and chmod into /sbin then rm -rf of the same path within ten seconds. On the network, flag outbound TCP/25 from processes that are not mail services, especially where the destination resolves to consumer-grade CPE. Check for PPTP on 1723 on edge appliances that have no business running it. Full IOC tables, cryptographic constants, host artifacts, and YARA rules are available in the Rapid7 report and in Rapid7's Intelligence Hub.  #DFIR_Radar

BraZetsu: a Brazilian 🇧🇷 Python-based IAB framework attributed to threat actor Exilware targets Iberian and Latin American corporate, financial, industrial, and law enforcement environments, feeding a commercial access marketplace since February 2026.  Key findings:  - BraZetsu is a modular, Python 3 framework compiled with Nuitka into standalone PE executables, a choice that defeats signature-based detection and complicates reverse engineering. At time of analysis, the latest v5 build was fully undetectable on VirusTotal. The framework retrieves its C2 config as a Base64, XOR-encrypted blob from Pastebin dead-drop resolvers (e.g., hxxps://pastebin[.]com/raw/aF0WCxia), decoded with the hardcoded key p4st3_s3cr3t_k3y, then parses the c2_domain, port, and auth_token from a pipe-delimited string. All C2 traffic runs over a persistent WebSocket connection on TLS port 8443, pointed at c2.installscenter[.]com and the VPS at 38.242.246[.]176.  - The framework's get_stealth_iab_tags function profiles every compromised host across roughly 20 categories: FINANCE_ERP (SAP, TOTVS/Protheus, Warsaw, Topaz, Diebold), SCADA_INDUSTRIAL (FactoryTalk, RSLogix, WinCC), BACKUP_SERVER (veeam.exe, bengine.exe), SECURITY_EDR (csfalconservice.exe for CrowdStrike, sentinelagent.exe for SentinelOne, msmpeng.exe for Defender), LAW_ENFORCEMENT (hostname prefixes PC-, PM-, DP-, SSP-), HEALTHCARE_HIS (Tasy ERP, DICOM port 104), and DEVOPS_CLOUD (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AZURE_CONFIG_DIR, KUBECONFIG). Profiled hosts are priced and listed on Infected Marketplace at infect[.]online and infectonline[.]store with a minimum deposit of roughly USD 5.80.  - Rather than stealing credentials or cookies, BraZetsu's get_browser_intel function copies Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Opera SQLite History databases to %TEMP% using shutil.copyfile to bypass file locks, then runs the query SELECT url, title, visit_count FROM urls WHERE url LIKE ? against a TARGET_DOMAINS list of approximately 230 domains spanning banking, ERP, e-commerce, and government portals. The function ler_e_preparar_certificados recursively hunts the user profile and OneDrive for .pfx and .p12 digital certificates and exfiltrates them bundled in a dossier. The function obter_identidade_v8 uses regex to extract CPF and CNPJ legal identifiers. File extensions actively hunted include .cnab, .240, .400, .rem, and .ret.  - Log strings embedded in the code reference a server-side AI engine: "Coleta metadados de hardware e porte da máquina para a IA do servidor" and "Define se o arquivo é um alvo prioritário para a IA." The volume of emoji-annotated Portuguese 🇵🇹 logging ([], [], []) is consistent with LLM-assisted development. The framework tracks as AgenteV2 in prior ANY.RUN reporting, sharing loader names wifi_driver.exe and msedge04.exe, payload temp_agente.dll (equivalent to agenteV2_historico_detect.dll), identical Python 3.13 plus Nuitka build environments, and the same 38.242.246[.]176 VPS. Persistence in v1 was established via a Run key named MonitorSystem under SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.  - Initial distribution runs through the domain caixaentradas1inboxshop[.]site using VBS droppers masquerading as a judicial notification ("processo de intimação") and file patterns msdege[0-9].exe and wifi_driver.exe. The same infrastructure distributed the Ousaban banking trojan. Buyers on Infected Marketplace can remotely execute their own payloads against purchased accesses via the _execute_worker function, creating a persistent threat-multiplication effect. Two US 🇺🇸 compromised hosts appeared for sale in April 2026, a potential indicator of geographic expansion.  Hunt priority: search endpoints running TOTVS, SAP, Senior, or Tasy for processes spawning cmd.exe (T1059.003) with WebSocket connections to external IPs on port 8443, and audit %TEMP% for copies of Chrome and Edge History SQLite databases alongside a file named debug_payload_sent.json. Flag outbound connections to Pastebin from hosts running ERP or SCADA software. Full IOC list including 16 file hashes, C2 domains, and Pastebin resolver URLs is in the Group-IB report. MITRE ATT&CK coverage spans T1012, T1083, T1217, T1113, T1027.002, and T1564.003 among others.  #DFIR_Radar

🚨 Detection Rule Friday: Suspicious Parent-Child Process Relationships  If you see winword.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe, you're likely looking at a maldoc in action. If svchost.exe has any parent other than services.exe, you've got injection or masquerading.  Process lineage is one of the most reliable detection primitives we have. Attackers abuse trusted binaries (LOLBins) to blend in, but they can't hide the parent-child relationship that reveals how execution really started.  Detection Logic: Query Sysmon Event ID 1 or Security 4688 with process creation details. Filter for high-risk parent-child pairs: • Microsoft Office processes (winword.exe, excel.exe, outlook.exe) spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe • svchost.exe with ParentImage != services.exe • explorer.exe spawning scripting engines from unusual paths • Legitimate system binaries (regsvr32.exe, rundll32.exe) launched by Office apps or browsers  Log Sources: • Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) with ParentImage field • Windows Security Event 4688 with ParentProcessName (requires command-line logging enabled)  False Positives & Tuning: Legitimate macro-enabled workflows exist in some enterprises. Build a whitelist of known-good parent-child pairs specific to your environment. Document approved automation scripts. Exclude service accounts running scheduled tasks that spawn shells. Use process hashes or signing info to differentiate legitimate from suspicious instances of the same binary name.  MITRE ATT&CK: T1204.002 (User Execution: Malicious File), T1036 (Masquerading)  Start with a baseline of normal process trees in your environment, then alert on deviations. This catches everything from phishing maldocs to post-exploitation tooling.  #DetectionEngineering #DFIR

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has been turned into a specialized local cybersecurity agent.  Meet RavenX-CyberAgent from deadbydawn101, a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model distilled around Opus-style reasoning and tuned specifically for penetration testing and security research.  The interesting part isn’t just the “uncensored” label.  It’s the workflow the model is designed around.  RavenX is built to work more like a security analyst than a general-purpose chatbot.  It focuses on things like:  Recon and tool-call style workflows Attack-surface analysis Structured security reporting MITRE ATT&CK mapping CWE classification CVSS scoring Pentest documentation  It also uses a RATH-style reporting structure designed to take security findings through the broader assessment process, from identifying the attack surface through analysis, impact, remediation and documentation.  That specialization matters.  A general coding model might be able to explain a vulnerability.  A cybersecurity-focused model can instead be trained to organize the surrounding workflow: what was observed, how the finding should be categorized, what technique it maps to, how severe it is and how the result should be documented.  And because RavenX is based on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, it has an interesting local footprint for a model in this class.  It’s a MoE architecture with roughly 36B total parameters but only around 3B active parameters per token.  The reported configuration supports a large context window, tool calling and GGUF deployment, making it much more practical for local security workflows than a massive dense model.  The model was reportedly trained across hundreds of thousands of security examples covering areas such as penetration testing, bug bounty reports, MITRE ATT&CK and other security-focused material.  That gives it a very different target from a normal coding assistant.  You could use a model like this as a local layer around an authorized security workflow, where it helps turn raw observations into structured findings instead of sending sensitive assessment data to an external API.  That’s probably the most interesting part of specialized local cyber models.  Privacy.  A security assessment can contain source code, internal hostnames, vulnerability details, logs, credentials accidentally exposed in output and other information you may not want leaving your environment.  Running the reasoning layer locally gives security teams another option.  Of course, “uncensored” doesn’t automatically mean “accurate.”  Cybersecurity is an area where confidently wrong output can be worse than a refusal.  So the real test for RavenX isn’t whether it answers offensive questions.  It’s whether it can reliably analyze authorized assessment data, use tools correctly, classify findings and produce reports that a human security professional can actually verify.  That’s where specialized models are getting interesting.  We’re moving from generic LLMs that happen to know cybersecurity toward models designed around complete security workflows.  Qwen3.6-35B-A3B provides the base.  The post-training provides the specialization.  Tool calling provides the agent layer.  And local deployment provides the privacy and control.  The next benchmark I want to see is straightforward:  Put RavenX through a controlled, authorized lab environment and measure how well it handles reconnaissance, evidence collection, finding classification, remediation guidance and final reporting from start to finish.  That’s a much more useful test than simply asking whether a cyber model can talk about hacking.

Towards Hierarchical Cyber Defense with Large Language Models: From Planning to Execution: An autonomous cyber defender trained with reinforcement learning (RL) is typically tied to the network on which it was trained, limiting its ability to generalize as network scale changes. Hierarchical RL reduces decision complexity by separating strategic targeting from tactical execution, but it does not eliminate this retraining dependence. We investigate whether frozen, zero-shot large language models (LLMs) can provide retraining-free control in hierarchical cyber defense and how performance changes as LLM control is extended from planning to execution. We formulate a controller-agnostic planner-executor hierarchy in which the planner selects a subnet to defend over a fixed horizon and the executor selects defensive actions within that subnet. Using the high fidelity Cyberwheel environment, with its built-in automated red team agent mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, we compare RL+RL, LLM+RL, and LLM+LLM configurations using six models ranging from 3B to 70B parameters, including two cybersecurity-specialized models, across small, medium, and large networks. Replacing only the planner with an LLM yields limited gains as network size increases. In contrast, extending LLM control to execution produces notable improvements for sufficiently capable models. For instance, a frozen general purpose 70B model holds successful lateral movement to approximately 1% of steps and attacker impact near zero across all three network scales using the same model weights, while the RL baseline is retrained for each scale. Our results show that sufficiently capable frozen LLMs can maintain strong defensive performance across the evaluated network scales without task-specific retraining, while also indicating that strong tactical execution is important to realizing the benefits of LLM-based control.ift.tt/7RLpjeq

I want my Christian friends to recognize a troubling pattern: the political manipulation of religion doesn't end with colonial history. We need to examine how it continues today, including here in the United States.  When I share concerns about Pakistani textbooks portraying Christianity through the lens of colonialism, I'm also asking us to examine how American policies and political rhetoric have portrayed Islam.  Religious discrimination doesn't become acceptable simply because our own government is involved.  I want people to understand how political leaders can exploit religious identity, fear and historical grievances. These practices can deepen divisions, expose innocent believers to hostility and create grievances that extremist movements may exploit.  We should examine these issues consistently, regardless of which religion is being targeted or which government is responsible.  I'm sharing these posts because I believe we cannot defend religious freedom selectively. Protecting Christians abroad and protecting Muslims at home are part of the same commitment to human dignity.  I've included the following articles and official documents so readers can examine the evidence themselves. I have not been active on Crypto this past weeks but somehow got the information days go; Something happened to Bitget Crypto Exchange platform; they got hacked.   380$ million apparently stolen. How did the hacker made it happen? Fingers points to North Korea hacking group, DPRK, Lazarus at it again probably.  Security, Check, Verify transactions is still very important.  What apparently happened According to the latest forensic information from Bitget's investigation, Mandiant and SlowMist:  The attackers first compromised a third-party security appliance used by Bitget. Mandiant reportedly found a zero-day vulnerability in that third-party security product. The attackers obtained privileged access, installed a web shell, established command-and-control access, and then moved laterally into Bitget's production wallet infrastructure.  They got into the backend system rather than directly stealing the wallet's private keys. This is the important part. Bitget says its private keys weren't compromised and its cold wallets weren't affected. Instead, the attackers manipulated transaction information inside the wallet backend.  They essentially made fraudulent transactions look legitimate to Bitget's own authorization system. Think of it like this: Normal: Backend says: "Transfer $100M → authorized destination" → security checks → sign → transfer.  Attack: Hacker alters the backend's transaction data → system sees what appears to be an authorized transaction → signing/authorization process proceeds → blockchain executes it. So even very strong private-key security doesn't necessarily save you if the software deciding what you're supposed to sign has been compromised.   They apparently tested the defenses first. Bitget's CEO said the attackers initially made two small transfers — 0.184 ETH and 193 TRX — that were below the exchange's risk-control thresholds. About 30 minutes later, they began the huge transfers.  Then they moved extremely quickly. Around 17 large transactions across multiple blockchains moved hundreds of millions of dollars. Chainalysis says about $387 million left Bitget in 23 transfers within the first three hours, across Ethereum, XRP, Zcash and Tron.

DPRK THREAT-ACTOR PLAYBOOK  North Korea runs its cyber operations like a state budget line. Patient, persistent, and above all, financially motivated in ways that distinguish it from almost every other state actor.  The archive holds 130 documented incidents spanning September 1996 to September 2026. Thirty years of continuous operation. The program did not emerge fully formed; it grew alongside the regime's nuclear ambitions, and the two are now structurally linked. Sanctions constrain hard currency. Cyber operations generate it.  ---  METHODS AND VOLUME  Cyber Espionage: 65 incidents Advanced Persistent Threat Operations: 60 incidents Critical Infrastructure Mapping: 26 incidents Infrastructure Attacks: 24 incidents Malware Distribution: 18 incidents Ransomware Campaigns: 17 incidents Cryptocurrency Theft: 17 incidents Supply Chain Exploitation: 16 incidents  The top two categories overlap considerably by design. DPRK APT operations are the delivery mechanism; espionage is frequently the payload. What separates North Korea from most state actors is what sits below that: cryptocurrency theft and ransomware running in parallel with traditional espionage. Pyongyang does not draw a clean line between intelligence collection and revenue generation. Sometimes the same access serves both purposes.  Critical infrastructure mapping at 26 incidents deserves attention. That number does not represent 26 attacks. It represents 26 instances of documented reconnaissance. The attacks, if they come, come later.  ---  HOW THEY WORK  The operational signature is patience and cover. North Korean operators routinely maintain access inside target networks for months before doing anything visible. When they do move, it is often to exfiltrate, occasionally to steal funds, and in a smaller number of cases to stage for potential disruptive action.  The social engineering tradecraft is unusually developed. Operation Dream Job, documented as recently as August 2026, has been running in recognizable form for years. The premise is simple: contact a defense or technology sector employee, pose as a recruiter, build rapport, deliver a malicious file or link embedded in what looks like a job application process. The August 2026 iteration added CVE-2026-68820, a Windows kernel privilege escalation zero-day, to the lure chain. Same concept, meaningfully upgraded technical execution.  That combination, a well-worn social engineering framework married to fresh exploit development, is characteristic. DPRK operators are not purely tool-reusers and they are not purely capability developers. They blend.  Supply chain exploitation appears in 16 documented incidents. That number has been climbing. The logic is straightforward: compromise a vendor with broad customer access once, and the downstream reach multiplies the effort. North Korean operators have applied this across software distribution channels, managed service providers, and development toolchains.  ---  THE FINANCIAL DIMENSION  This is where North Korea differs structurally from China, Russia, or Iran.  Seventeen documented cryptocurrency theft incidents. Seventeen documented ransomware campaigns. These are not side projects. UN Panel of Experts assessments have repeatedly found that DPRK cyber operations fund prohibited weapons programs directly. The Lazarus Group and affiliated clusters have been attributed to cryptocurrency platform compromises totaling billions of dollars across multiple years. The September 2026 Security Affairs Round 597 digest captured continued activity in this space alongside document exfiltration operations, which is a good illustration of how the programs run concurrently rather than sequentially.  Ransomware as espionage cover is a documented pattern. Deploy ransomware, collect payment, but the primary objective was data access. The ransom demand provides both revenue and a convenient explanation for the intrusion that does not require the victim to acknowledge what was actually taken.  ---  INSTITUTIONAL ARCHITECTURE  North Korea's cyber operations sit under Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), which also controls foreign intelligence and special operations. The organizational consolidation matters because it means cyber, signals, and human intelligence operations can be coordinated at the command level rather than deconflicted after the fact.  Lazarus Group is the most publicly attributed cluster, but the attribution landscape is segmented. Bluenoroff handles financial operations. Andariel has been associated with critical infrastructure targeting and ransomware. APT38 (overlapping with Bluenoroff in many frameworks) focuses on financial system intrusions. In practice the clusters share infrastructure and personnel, and the boundaries in public reporting reflect analytic conventions more than hard operational divisions.  ---  RECENT INDICATORS  The September 2026 DPRK Foreign Ministry statement is worth treating as a data point, not just diplomatic noise. Pyongyang issues sovereignty doctrine statements in coordinated patterns. They function as preemptive rhetorical cover for activities the regime knows will attract scrutiny, and they are systematically amplified through Russian and Chinese state media. The September 2026 statement coincided with documented DPRK weapons and personnel provision to Russia for Ukraine operations, an alignment that has material implications for technology transfer and operational coordination between the programs.  The Tenable-SentinelOne joint analysis from August 2026, covering 93 CVE-actor pairs, found state APTs and criminal actors converging on identical edge infrastructure vulnerabilities. North Korean operators appear in that dataset. The convergence is a deliberate feature in some cases. When your intrusion looks indistinguishable from a criminal ransomware operator's intrusion, attribution slows and the intelligence or financial objective proceeds.  The FBI's September 2026 global threat framework names North Korea alongside China, Russia, and Iran in multi-domain operations against U.S. interests. North Korea does not lead that assessment in terms of overall threat volume. China holds that position. But the FBI framework documents DPRK operations spanning espionage, economic theft, and what the framework terms transnational repression, meaning operations against North Korean diaspora communities and defectors abroad. That last category is underreported relative to its actual frequency.  ---  WHAT TO WATCH  Three things.  First, the Dream Job template keeps evolving. It has absorbed zero-days before and it will again. Any organization in defense, aerospace, technology, or cryptocurrency that is not actively training employees on this specific social engineering vector has a gap.  Second, the Russia alignment is not cosmetic. DPRK provision of artillery, missiles, and reportedly personnel to Russia creates conditions for reciprocal technology transfer. If Russian cyber tooling or infrastructure begins appearing in DPRK operations at higher frequency, that alignment has moved beyond weapons logistics.  Third, cryptocurrency infrastructure remains a primary target. North Korean operators have demonstrated the ability to compromise exchange platforms, DeFi protocols, and individual custody solutions. The sophistication of these operations has increased year over year. The seventeen incidents in the archive represent confirmed attributions. The actual number is higher.  Thirty years in, the program is larger, better resourced, and more technically capable than it was at any prior point. The financial motive is structural, not opportunistic. It does not go away when diplomatic conditions shift, because the weapons programs the revenue funds do not pause for diplomacy either.  foreigninterference.org #foreigninterference #CyberEspionage #AdvancedPersistentThreatOperations #CriticalInfrastructureMapping #InfrastructureAttacks

🚨TIMELINES, PATTERNS, THE ILLEGAL ILLICIT NETWORK & ANOTHER "UNPRECEDENTED" EVENT  👉Ninety-One Billion Dollars  On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury designated the A7 Network as a significant transnational criminal organization.  The A7 Network processed more than 2,000 transactions per day. Its total transaction volume exceeded 7.5 trillion rubles $91.5 billion. That represents approximately 13% of Russia's entire foreign trade in 2025. One network. Thirteen percent of a G20 economy's international commerce.  Treasury deployed three instruments simultaneously.  FinCEN issued a proposed rule prohibiting any transmittal of funds involving A7 Sub-Agents. That's the plumbing-level ban every bank in the world is now on notice that processing a payment through an A7 entity is a potential violation.  FinCEN issued an Alert with red flags to help financial institutions identify A7 activity. That's the map handed to the private sector the same FinCEN Exchange mechanism that briefed banks on Operation Economic Outcast two weeks ago.  OFAC designated the entire A7 Network as a transnational criminal organization. That's the nuclear option every asset, every entity, every Sub-Agent, every transaction blocked.  Three tools. One target. One press release. One morning.  Here's what the A7 Network actually is.  A constellation of purpose-built shell companies called "Sub-Agents" spread across third-country jurisdictions. Each Sub-Agent is designed to receive and send payments that make sanctioned transactions look like ordinary commerce. Falsified trade documents. Falsified import-export records. Misleading goods descriptions. The entire architecture exists to make illegal payments invisible inside the legitimate financial system.  The Sub-Agents' websites and bank accounts are controlled by A7 Network staff using custom-built VPNs that mask their true location. The companies are shells. The websites are facades. The bank accounts are funnels. The VPNs hide who's actually pressing the buttons.  This isn't a few bad actors using the financial system. This is a parallel financial system, purpose-built to evade the one that every government in the world has spent two decades making transparent.  Now read who used it.  Russia 13% of its foreign trade flowed through A7's infrastructure.  Iran  the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC used A7 Sub-Agents to move funds through the international financial system.  Hamas  A7 facilitated transactions for Iran-backed terrorist organizations, including Hamas.  North Korea  A7 Sub-Agents facilitated transactions related to North Korean hacks of cryptocurrency exchanges.  Ransomware operators cybercriminals used A7 to move funds.  Iran's shadow fleet  one A7 Sub-Agent directly transacted with tankers, shipping companies, and front companies used to transport and sell Iranian oil in violation of sanctions. That same Sub-Agent received nearly $140 million from Iranian sanctions evaders.  Iranian weapons procurement a separate Sub-Agent transferred $1.6 million to a company linked to Iranian weapons procurement.  Every adversary this series has documented. Russia. Iran. IRGC. Hamas. North Korea. Ransomware. All of them. Through the same pipes. At the same time.  The network even built its own cryptocurrency.  The A7A5 token a ruble-backed digital token issued by Old Vector LLC, which OFAC designated in August 2025. Created specifically for A7 members to evade sanctions and transact internationally. A purpose-built sanctions evasion cryptocurrency.  Three weeks ago, this series documented a cartel mining farm in the mountains of Puebla 300 GPUs making coins from stolen electricity because the existing crypto rails were being monitored. The A7 Network did the same thing at the institutional level it built its own token because existing tokens were being screened.  When the transparent rail gets too transparent, the adversary builds a parallel rail. When the parallel rail gets designated, the adversary builds a token for the parallel rail. Each layer of evasion produces a new layer of enforcement. Each layer of enforcement produces a new layer of evasion.  $17 billion processed between January 2025 and June 2026. Eighteen months.  $91.5 billion in total transaction volume. Thirteen percent of Russia's foreign trade.  $140 million received from Iranian sanctions evaders by a single Sub-Agent.  2,000 transactions per day.  Those numbers existed inside the global financial system. They moved through banks. They cleared through payment networks. They appeared on ledgers as ordinary commercial activity. And the entire time, the money was flowing from Russia to Iran to Hamas to North Korea to ransomware operators through a network of shell companies controlled by a convicted criminal fraudster named Ilan Shor, operating from behind custom VPNs across multiple jurisdictions.  The transparent rail caught it. FinCEN mapped it. OFAC designated it. The Alert went out to every financial institution in the world. The proposed rule will prohibit any bank from processing A7 payments. The UK's National Crime Agency flagged $86 billion in A7-linked flows in August. And today Treasury tore the whole thing up by the roots.  Yesterday, the last American soldier left Iraq. Today, Treasury designated a $91.5 billion shadow banking network that served every adversary on earth.  The rifle went home. The pen went to work. And the pen found $91.5 billion moving through purpose-built shell companies, falsified trade documents, and a custom cryptocurrency serving Russia, Iran, Hamas, North Korea, and ransomware operators through the same pipes, at the same time, disguised as ordinary commerce.  Follow the pen.  The source is the U.S. Department of the Treasury, Press Release sb0644, October 1, 2026.  I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

“온체인에 올리기만 하면 팔린다?…RWA도 이용자부터 알아야”  [STO써밋 2026] 크리스 인 플룸네트워크 대표 거래소·네오뱅크·디파이 연계 유통 전략 제시 “기존 상품 그대로 옮겨선 투자자 끌어오기 어려워” "한국 금융상품·문화자산, 해외 투자자 접근성 높여야"  실물연계자산(RWA) 시장에서 성과를 내려면 기존 금융상품을 블록체인으로 옮기는 데 그치지 않고 이용자의 수요와 투자 방식에 맞춰 상품과 유통 경로를 바꿔야 한다는 제언이 나왔다.  투자자가 이미 이용하는 거래소와 금융서비스에서 토큰화 자산에 접근할 수 있어야 실제 자금 유입으로 이어진다는 설명이다.  크리스 인 플룸네트워크 공동창업자 겸 대표는 1일 서울 여의도 한국거래소(KRX) 컨퍼런스홀에서 열린 '이데일리 STO 써밋 2026'에서 '차세대 RWA: 실물자산의 온체인화'를 주제로 발표하며 이같이 밝혔다.  인 대표는 "대부분은 기존 상품을 그대로 온체인에 올려놓고 잘 작동하기를 바라지만 실제로는 그렇지 않다"며 "유통과 이용자를 먼저 고려해야 온체인에서 실질적인 가치를 만들어낼 수 있다"고 말했다.   온체인은 자산의 발행과 거래 등을 블록체인상에서 처리하는 방식을 뜻한다.  인 대표는 맥도날드의 해외 진출을 예로 들었다. 같은 햄버거를 팔더라도 국가별로 메뉴와 매장 경험을 달리하듯 금융상품도 새로운 시장의 이용자가 무엇을 원하고 어떤 방식으로 상품을 이용하는지 파악해야 한다는 설명이다.  그는 자산을 온체인에 발행하고 대대적으로 홍보해도 실제 투자자금이 들어오지 않는 사례가 많다고 지적했다.   상품을 먼저 내놓고 수요가 생기기를 기다리기보다 이용자와 유통 경로를 파악한 뒤 이에 맞춰 상품을 설계해야 한다고 강조했다.  RWA 시장의 성장 여건으로는 스테이블코인 시장 확대와 규제 변화, 국제 정세 불안에 따른 자금 이동을 꼽았다.   인 대표는 "온체인 스테이블코인 규모는 3000억 달러(약 407조원)를 넘어섰고 이제는 관심을 가질 만큼 충분히 큰 시장이 됐다"며 "국제 정세 불안으로 자금과 사업 거점을 옮기려는 움직임도 나타나고 있다"고 말했다.  국경과 거래 시간의 제약을 줄일 수 있다는 점도 토큰화의 이점으로 꼽았다.   투자자가 여러 국가와 자산군에 자금을 배분하기 쉬워지고 금융회사도 해외 고객을 확보할 기회가 커진다는 설명이다.  인 대표는 "24시간 운영되는 국제 시장에서는 전 세계에서 자금과 자산을 훨씬 빠르게 옮길 수 있다"며 "기업들도 전 세계를 대상으로 경쟁하고 사업을 펼칠 수 있다”고 말했다.  이어 "기존에는 세계적인 대형 자산운용사를 따라잡아야 했다"며 "온체인에 새로운 시장이 만들어진다면 신생 기업도 그 기회를 활용해 이용자를 확보할 수 있다"고 덧붙였다.  실제 투자 수요를 확보할 유통 경로로는 중앙화 거래소와 네오뱅크(인터넷 은행), 탈중앙화금융(DeFi, 디파이) 프로토콜을 제시했다. 중앙화 거래소에는 스테이블코인 자금이 모여 있고, 네오뱅크는 이를 일상 결제에 쓰려는 수요를 바탕으로 성장하고 있다고 설명했다.  인 대표는 "규모를 키우려면 가장 중요한 것은 자금이 어디에 얼마나 있는지 파악하는 일"이라며 "스테이블코인을 쓰기 위해 네오뱅크로 자금을 옮기는 사람이 많아지면서 이 분야가 빠르게 성장하고 있다"고 말했다.  디파이 대출 시장에 대해서는 상대적으로 자금 규모가 작지만 새로운 금융서비스를 실험하는 곳으로 평가했다. 이곳에서 시작한 서비스가 거래소와 네오뱅크로 확산할 수 있다는 설명이다.  인 대표는 "온체인 대출 시장은 자금 규모가 아주 크지는 않지만 많은 실험이 시작되는 곳"이라며 "원하는 시장과 이용자에게 도달하려면 세 영역에 모두 진출해야 한다"고 강조했다.  투자자의 신뢰도 주요 과제로 꼽았다. 인 대표는 "해킹 사고가 이어지면서 이용자들은 안전하다고 느끼는 몇몇 서비스로 모이려 한다"며 "이용자들이 모인 곳에서 상품을 제공하는 것이 가장 중요하다"고 말했다.  한국 금융회사의 해외 진출 가능성도 강조했다. 기존에는 해외에 금융상품을 공급하려면 현지 법인을 설립하거나 별도 상장 절차를 밟아야 해 시간과 비용이 많이 들었다는 설명이다.  인 대표는 "온체인에서는 기존 국내 시장에 금융상품을 공급하면서 미국과 중남미, 유럽 등으로 시장을 넓힐 수 있다"며 "한국 기업도 한 시장에서만 상품을 파는 대신 여러 시장에 진출해 매출을 늘리고 글로벌 브랜드로 성장할 기회가 있다"고 말했다.  한국 자산에 대한 해외 투자자의 접근성을 높여야 한다는 점도 짚었다. 한국은 개인투자자와 금융산업 기반이 탄탄하고 금융상품뿐 아니라 문화·미디어 분야에서도 해외 수요가 높다고 평가했다.  인 대표는 "한국의 문화와 미디어는 이미 세계적으로 인기가 높다"며 "이런 자산을 금융상품으로 만들고 해외 투자자가 접근할 수 있도록 하면 해외로 나가는 자금 대신 국내로 들어오는 자금을 크게 늘릴 수 있다"고 말했다.  🗞n.news.naver.com/article/018…

Kraken - Ink, Bybit- Mantle 등도 이런 것이 필요하고 USDT와 Layer Zero등의 기술이 이런것을 가능하게 하는 것을 볼 수 있었습니다.  업비트측 : 기관들이 최근에 웹3 유즈케이스를 찾는데 집중하고 있습니다. 몇년 전만해도 유럽이나 한국의 기관들은 POC나 MOU만 하는데, 업비트가 기와를 론칭하면서 기관들을 연락하려고 했는데, 오히려 기관들이 먼저 연락을 할 정도로 적극적이였습니다. 그리고 업비트가 웹3 생태계를 만드는데 진심이라는 것을 볼 수 있었습니다. 그럼에도 웹3로 온보딩 하면 파편화의 문제는 그대로 있다는것입니다. 이유는 기관들이 그들만의 생태계를 만드려고 하는 기본적인 움직임이 있기 때문입니다.   그래서 현재는 네트워크상에서 POC등을 하는 것이 중요하다고 생각함.   3. 기와 체인과 지갑은 유동성 파편화에 어떻게 도움됨? - Alex  한국 사용자들이 상당히 흥미로운게 리테일이 매우 강하고 트레이딩을 좋아한다는 것입니다. 그런데 대부분 크립토 네이티브가 아닌 CEX에서 머문다는 것입니다.   몇 가지 이유는 신뢰에 대한 부분이고, 크립토에 대해서 부정적인것도 있고 (스캠, 러그, 해킹 등등등... 이건 제이의 생각) 그래서 이것을 도와주려고 했고, 해외 시스템 가지 말고 그냥 기와 이용해서 월렛등으로 "안전하게" 업비트에서 입출금하고 사용할 수 있는 환경을 만드는 것이라고 함.
